headline_en: Four Bangladeshi brothers die of gas in a car in Oman
summary_en: Four Bangladeshi brothers from Rangunia died in Oman after inhaling carbon monoxide from the AC exhaust of a running car. Royal Oman Police are investigating and warned against sleeping in closed cars. The bodies are due to reach Chattogram and the Chattogram Samity Oman and the Bangladesh embassy are working on repatriation.

facts.statement: Four Bangladeshi brothers (Rashedul, Shahedul, Sirajul and Shahidul) from a poor family in Rangunia died in Oman from inhaling carbon monoxide gas emitted from the AC exhaust while their car's engine was running.
After four Bangladeshi brothers died of carbon monoxide in a running car in Oman, the Royal Oman Police opened an investigation and issued a warning not to sleep in a closed car.

facts.date: 2026-05-19 (the coming Tuesday after publication on 16 May 2026)
facts.statement: The bodies of the four brothers who died in Oman (Rashedul, Shahedul, Sirajul, Shahidul) were due to arrive in Chattogram on the coming Tuesday; Chattogram Samity Oman and the Bangladesh embassy were working to send the bodies home.
The mother of the four brothers who died in Oman, Khadija Begum of Rangunia, had not yet been told of her sons' deaths when the article was published.

headline_en: Rabeya of Faridpur wins a motorcycle in Krishi Bank's remittance festival
summary_en: Rabeya, wife of Malaysia-based migrant Md. Mominul Shikdar of Shibchar, Madaripur, won the mega prize motorcycle in Bangladesh Krishi Bank's remittance festival lottery after he sent BDT 205,000 to her account. The festival ran 40 days around Eid-ul-Fitr and 39 prizes were drawn among recipients of remittance sent through the bank.

facts.statement: Bangladesh Krishi Bank held a 40-day 'remittance festival' for Eid-ul-Fitr from 19 February to 30 March (2026); people who received remittance sent by migrants through Krishi Bank in that period were entered in a lottery, and winners were chosen for a total of 39 prizes.

Rabeya, wife of Malaysia-based migrant Md. Mominul Shikdar of Shibchar upazila, Madaripur, won the mega prize (a motorcycle) in the Krishi Bank remittance festival lottery after her husband sent BDT 2 lakh 5 thousand as remittance to her account at the bank's Bajitpur branch at Sheikhpur Bazar, Shibchar; the motorcycle was handed over on Wednesday 6 May 2026 at the branch by Mohammad Moinul Islam, general manager of the bank's Faridpur divisional office.
Bangladesh Krishi Bank has 1,038 branches across the country; the Bajitpur branch customer Rabeya was selected first among them in the remittance festival draw.
Rabeya said she did not believe it when she first heard she had won the Krishi Bank remittance lottery; bank officials later came to her home to confirm it.

summary_en: At the 'Migrant Conference 2026' organised by OKUP at Probashi Kalyan Bhaban in Dhaka, State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare Nurul Haque Nur spoke almost entirely about domestic politics and social media. The article lists the migration-sector officials who spoke and says migrant workers discussed their experiences abroad, but gives no migration detail.

headline_en: Migration abroad reduces the risk of poverty
summary_en: Research presented at SANEM's annual economists' conference in Dhaka found that Bangladeshi households with a member working abroad face a lower risk of poverty and coped better with Covid-19 and post-Ukraine-war inflation than internal-migrant households. Other papers covered climate-driven internal migration in coastal areas and a Bangladesh Bank study finding no 'Dutch disease' from remittances so far.

facts.statement: A study by Mahtab Uddin, assistant professor of economics at Dhaka University, on the impact of Covid-19 and post Russia-Ukraine war inflation on migrant households found that households with members working abroad are at comparatively lower risk of poverty and withstood the Covid shock well, while internal migrants struggle with economic shocks.
facts.source_in_article: Mahtab Uddin, Dhaka University, at the SANEM annual economists' conference

facts.statement: The study found international migrant households are much less likely than internal migrant households to fall below the poverty line because their income is higher; Mahtab Uddin said remittance works like a shield, so the households can absorb price rises and have better food quality and nutrition security than others.

A Bangladesh Bank study presented by additional director Ripon Roy found that although theory predicts 'Dutch disease' when remittance rises, this tendency has not been seen in Bangladesh so far and rising remittance is not reducing export competitiveness; he said remittance money is not spent only on consumption but accumulates as capital and is invested in education and health, and advised examining how to use it more in productive sectors.
facts.source_in_article: Ripon Roy, additional director, Bangladesh Bank

facts.statement: A World Bank and BIDS jointly funded survey of 403 coastal households, presented by BIDS senior research fellow Azreen Karim, found (preliminary results) that sudden disasters such as floods or cyclones lead to partial migration (about 40 percent), with able members leaving for work while others stay, whereas slow disasters like river erosion push whole families to migrate; this is internal migration within Bangladesh.

The findings were presented on Sunday 19 April 2026 at BRAC Centre Inn, Mohakhali, Dhaka, on the closing day of the three-day annual economists' conference of the South Asian Network on Economic Modeling (SANEM); the session was chaired by Rahnuma Salam Khan, national programme manager of ILO Bangladesh.

headline_en: We are working to open the Malaysian labour market quickly: Prime Minister's adviser
summary_en: Mahdi Amin, the Prime Minister's adviser on expatriates' welfare and overseas employment and spokesperson of the Prime Minister's Office, said the government is working to reopen the closed Malaysian labour market as fast as possible. He said Bangladesh has asked Malaysia to do whatever is needed to make the process syndicate-free, transparent and low-cost.

facts.statement: As of 12 April 2026 the Malaysian labour market was closed to Bangladeshi workers; Mahdi Amin, the Prime Minister's adviser on expatriates' welfare and overseas employment and spokesperson of the Prime Minister's Office, said reopening is a procedural matter and the government is working to open it as quickly as possible, without giving a date.
facts.source_in_article: Mahdi Amin, Prime Minister's adviser, speaking to journalists at the Secretariat

facts.statement: Mahdi Amin said Bangladesh wants people to be able to go to Malaysia at low cost through a transparent process and has called on Malaysia to do whatever is necessary to make the process syndicate-free; he said both the Bangladeshi and Malaysian prime ministers have shown sincerity on this.

Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury and adviser Mahdi Amin recently visited Malaysia and held discussions with policymakers there about sending Bangladeshi workers.

headline_en: Migrants from the Middle East get a chance to renew visas
summary_en: With flights disrupted by the Iran versus US-Israel attacks, many migrants on leave in Bangladesh are stuck with visas expiring. The Expatriates' Welfare Ministry issued a public notice saying workers from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, UAE, Oman and Bahrain can seek visa renewal through their employer or kafil, or apply online, and that Kuwait, Qatar and UAE have extended expired or expiring visas by one month.

facts.statement: A public notice from the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment said workers who came to Bangladesh from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Oman and Bahrain can contact their employer or kafil to have their visa renewed, and can also apply online.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment public notice

facts.statement: According to the Bangladesh expatriates' welfare ministry notice, the governments of Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates extended by one month the visas of those whose visas had already expired or were about to expire.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment public notice

facts.statement: Qatar (with Kuwait and the UAE) extended by one month the validity of visas that had expired or were about to expire, according to the Bangladesh expatriates' welfare ministry notice issued during the Iran-Israel war situation.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment public notice

facts.statement: The UAE (with Kuwait and Qatar) extended by one month the validity of visas that had expired or were about to expire, according to the Bangladesh expatriates' welfare ministry notice issued during the Iran-Israel war situation.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment public notice

facts.statement: Because of the Iran and US-Israel exchange of attacks, international flights became irregular and many migrants who had come to Bangladesh on leave were stuck, some with visas expired and some close to expiry; the ministry said it was not possible for them to go to the destination country to renew, so an alternative arrangement was made.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment public notice

headline_en: 'The roar of the missiles terrifies us, we cannot sleep at night'
summary_en: Bangladeshi migrants from Madaripur living in Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Dubai describe fear, lost work and sleepless nights as Iranian missiles target US bases during the Middle East war. In Qatar many have no work as projects have stopped, two to three Bangladeshis were reportedly hurt by falling missile debris, and the Qatar government told everyone to stay indoors. A Madaripur manpower official says the ministry has a call centre and help will be given through embassies.

facts.statement: During the war in early March 2026 the Qatar government told everyone to stay indoors, because debris falls when missiles are intercepted in the sky and could injure people.

Migrants in Qatar said some Bangladeshis went out over-eagerly to see where missiles fell, collect missile debris and take photos and video, and two to three Bangladeshis were injured by missile debris falling from the sky.

Qatar-based migrant Irad Shikdar (40), an electric supervisor at a multinational company who has lived in Doha for over 12 years, said many Bangladeshis in Qatar have no work, projects are shut and people are struggling for food; he said 8 to 10 lakh Bengalis live in Qatar and all are in fear.
facts.source_in_article: Irad Shikdar, migrant in Doha, from Badamtala, Madaripur town

facts.statement: Siam Sardar (27) of Mohisherchar, Madaripur Sadar, who went to Qatar two and a half years earlier, said he cannot go to any work and is confined at home, and that he can see with his own eyes missiles landing on the American 'airways' (as printed: আমেরিকার এয়ারওয়েজে); attacks were intensifying day by day.

Migrant Hannan Molla (28) of Amirabad, Madaripur town, said four missiles fell in Qatar at about 8 pm on Tuesday (3 March 2026) and four more at about 1 am; Iran targets the US base in Qatar at unpredictable times including before iftar and in the morning; sirens used to sound before but no longer do, and explosions shake all of Doha.

Lokman Hossain (35) of Chargobindapur, Khoajpur union, Madaripur, who has lived with his family in Riyadh for a decade and works at a super shop, said panic spread when the US embassy in Saudi Arabia was hit by a drone attack; Bangladeshis are still working but in fear.

Delwar Hossain of Tantibari, Mostofapur union, Madaripur, who has lived in Dubai for 17 years, said loud explosions shake the whole building, he cannot sleep at night and keeps thinking where to take shelter.

Abdul Jalil Mia, assistant director of the Madaripur District Employment and Manpower Office, said the ministry has taken necessary steps to protect Bangladeshis in the Middle East and there is a call centre; if migrants seek help there, all kinds of assistance will be given through the embassy. No number is printed.
facts.source_in_article: Abdul Jalil Mia, assistant director, Madaripur District Employment and Manpower Office

facts.statement: The article says Madaripur is at the top among Bangladesh's migrant-heavy districts; most of its migrants are in Europe but many also work in Middle Eastern countries.
The eldest son of Omar Ali Shikdar, a newspaper agent in Madaripur, works in Qatar and was due to return home before Eid, but that became uncertain and he could not work because of the war.

headline_en: Give priority to the safety of expatriates
summary_en: A Prothom Alo editorial on the US-Israel attack on Iran and Iran's counter-strikes across the Middle East urges the government to prioritise the safety of Bangladeshis there. It notes two Bangladeshis killed (in the UAE and Bahrain), about 102 Dhaka to Middle East flights cancelled in three days, and thousands stranded with expiring visas.

facts.statement: Bangladeshi national Saleh Ahmed was among three people killed in an Iranian attack on the United Arab Emirates on Sunday (1 March 2026).
A Bangladeshi named Abul Mohsin was killed in Bahrain during the Iranian attacks; as of Monday 2 March 2026 two Bangladeshis in total were reported killed in the conflict.
The editorial says more than 50 lakh (5 million) expatriate Bangladeshis work in Middle Eastern countries.
A few hundred Bangladeshis including 300 students are in Iran; the foreign ministry said all were safe so far.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, cited in editorial

facts.statement: In three days about 102 Dhaka to Middle East flights were cancelled because of the conflict, and no one could come to Bangladesh from Middle Eastern countries; several thousand people suffered, many of them outbound workers whose visas were running out. The foreign ministry sought help from diplomats of several countries.

The US and Israel jointly began attacking Iran on Saturday (28 February 2026), killing Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and others; Iran then struck Israel and US bases, and attacked Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Jordan and other Middle Eastern countries.

The editorial says embassies should regularly advise Bangladeshis in Middle Eastern countries to avoid risky and conflict-prone areas, ensure treatment for the injured, prepare in advance to evacuate Bangladeshis from Iran, and the government should step up diplomacy so outbound workers do not fall into crisis over visa complications and look after passengers stranded at airports at home and in the Middle East.

headline_en: BDT 20,000 crore in remittance came through bKash in one year
summary_en: bKash said expatriates sent BDT 20,000 crore in remittance through it in 2025 to 41 lakh accounts, about double the previous year. It describes how remittance reaches bKash accounts with the government incentive, the ATM cash-out cost, and a new remittance statement service in the app.

facts.statement: In 2025 expatriate Bangladeshis sent BDT 20,000 crore in remittance through mobile financial service bKash into 41 lakh bKash accounts in total, about double the previous year.

bKash says migrants in more than 170 countries can send remittance to bKash through 135 international money transfer operators (MTOs); the money is settled through 27 banks in Bangladesh and reaches the recipient's bKash account with the government incentive of BDT 25 per thousand.
Remittance received in a bKash account can be cashed out at more than 2,500 ATM booths of partner banks across Bangladesh at a cost of BDT 7 per thousand.

The bKash app has added a 'remittance statement' service so migrants' relatives can easily get a statement of remittance received in their bKash account, which also helps in filing income tax returns.

From the bKash app, migrants' relatives can open a DPS (deposit pension scheme) with four banks and one financial institution, and can use remittance to pay utility bills, educational institution fees and shopping payments.

In 2025 expatriates sent about USD 33 billion in remittance to Bangladesh through banks, 22 percent more than in 2024; in the same period remittance sent through mobile financial services (MFS) grew by more than 90 percent.

headline_en: Women's labour is changing Habiganj's economy
summary_en: A feature on women's economic role in Habiganj (tea gardens, farming, factories, small business). One section reports that about 300 women from Dudhpatil village in Chunarughat work in Middle Eastern countries and their remittances have visibly changed the village, now called the 'village of migrant women'.

facts.statement: About 300 women from Dudhpatil village in Chunarughat upazila, Habiganj, work in various Middle Eastern countries and regularly send money home; their money has brought visible change in houses, land purchase and education, and locals now call Dudhpatil the 'village of migrant women'.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter; Mohammad Ali, chairman of Gazipur Union Parishad

facts.statement: Runa Khatun of Dudhpatil village, Chunarughat, Habiganj, has worked abroad for five years (country not named); with her own earnings she bought 12 decimals of land for BDT 12 lakh, built a house, and sent one brother and two sisters abroad for work.

Parvin Akter of Habiganj town, whose husband is a migrant in Saudi Arabia, started a tailoring business five years ago with BDT 20,000 savings and a BDT 20,000 loan from the Ichhamoti Sromojibi Mohila Samity of Habiganj Unnayan Sangstha; her business capital is now about BDT 20 lakh with 15 sewing machines and 15 to 20 women employed.
facts.source_in_article: Parvin Akter; Mohammad Shahin, executive director, Habiganj Unnayan Sangstha

headline_en: US tightens visas, remittances and travel
summary_en: The US added Bangladesh and 24 other countries to its visa bond list (38 countries in total), requiring B1/B2 visa applicants to post a refundable bond of USD 5,000, 10,000 or 15,000 and to enter and leave through three named airports; for newly added countries it takes effect on 21 January 2026. A 1 percent tax on cash remittance transfers from the US took effect on 1 January 2026. Analysts say both will discourage travel and push remittances to informal channels.

facts.statement: An extra tax of 1 dollar per 100 dollars on cash transactions for sending remittance from the United States to any country took effect from the first day of 2026, as previously announced.

On Tuesday 6 January 2026 the US State Department's travel website announced that nationals of 38 countries including Bangladesh must post a 'visa bond' (security deposit) of up to USD 15,000 when applying to enter the United States; the article gives this as about BDT 18 lakh 35 thousand at BDT 122.31 per dollar.
For the newly added countries including Bangladesh (with a few exceptions) the US visa bond condition takes effect from 21 January (2026).

The State Department says anyone travelling on a passport issued by a listed country who is found eligible for a B1/B2 (business and tourist) visa must post a bond of USD 5,000, 10,000 or 15,000; the amount is set at the visa interview.
Under the US visa bond rules the applicant must also submit Department of Homeland Security form 'I-352' and agree to the bond terms through the US Treasury's online payment platform 'Pay.gov'.
Paying the US visa bond does not guarantee a visa; the money is refunded if the visa application is refused or if the visa holder complies with all visa conditions.
Under the new rule all US visa applicants must attend an in-person interview.

Visa holders under the bond must enter and leave the United States through designated ports or may be refused entry or risk their departure not being recorded correctly; the designated airports are Boston Logan International (BOS), John F. Kennedy International (JFK) and Washington Dulles International (IAD). A correction notes the article first wrongly wrote 'Dallas airport'.

The US first put six countries on the visa bond list in August 2025, then added seven more, and on Tuesday 6 January 2026 added 25 more including Bangladesh, making 38; most are African, with some from Latin America and Asia.

The 25 countries newly put under the US visa bond are Bangladesh, Algeria, Angola, Antigua and Barbuda, Benin, Burundi, Cape Verde, Cuba, Djibouti, Dominica, Fiji, Gabon, Ivory Coast, Kyrgyzstan, Nepal, Nigeria, Senegal, Tajikistan, Togo, Tonga, Tuvalu, Uganda, Vanuatu, Venezuela and Zimbabwe; the 13 already listed are Bhutan, Botswana, Central African Republic, Gambia, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Malawi, Mauritania, Namibia, Sao Tome and Principe, Tanzania, Turkmenistan and Zambia.

The US visa bond is a 12-month pilot programme that began on 20 August (2025); the State Department's August notice said that since 2000 many foreigners who entered on visas have no departure record, showing thousands of non-immigrant visitors each year do not leave on time.

The US Department of Homeland Security told Congress that in fiscal year 2023 about 3 crore 90 lakh (39 million) visa holders were due to depart, but about 4 lakh people stayed in the US after their visas expired.
facts.source_in_article: US Department of Homeland Security report to Congress

facts.statement: On 4 January 2026 President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social a list 'Immigrant Welfare Recipient Rates by Country of Origin' covering 120 countries and territories; Bangladesh ranked 19th, with 54.8 percent of Bangladeshi immigrant households in the US shown as receiving government benefits.

The article says US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) policy was updated in August 2025 to tighten immigration; social-media vetting of immigration applications, which the article says the Trump administration introduced in June (2024, as printed), is to be widened to include searching for 'anti-American activities'.

M Humayun Kabir, former Bangladesh ambassador to the US and president of the Bangladesh Enterprise Institute, said the visa bond and the new tax on remittance will affect personal and family travel and obstruct normal people-to-people movement; Mustafizur Rahman of CPD said the tax on cash remittance may encourage sending through informal channels and the bond will make going to the US difficult.

Diplomatic sources in Dhaka and Washington said the Trump administration had repeatedly signalled informally to Bangladesh and other countries that it would get tough on people overstaying in the US and becoming irregular.
facts.source_in_article: Diplomatic sources in Dhaka and Washington

headline_en: Khaleda Zia is not physically fit to be taken abroad now: Mirza Fakhrul
OEP will give free services to workers wishing to go abroad
summary_en: An online platform called the Overseas Employment Platform (OEP) has been launched by the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry with ILO and Swiss government support. It is to help workers apply for overseas jobs and get BMET registration and clearance at no cost, linking recruiting agencies, BMET, TTCs, foreign employers and immigration authorities.

facts.statement: An online platform named 'Overseas Employment Platform (OEP)' has been launched at the initiative of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment with joint support from the ILO and the Government of Switzerland; it will help workers apply for jobs abroad and obtain BMET registration and clearance ('ছাড়পত্র') free of cost.
Recruiting agencies, BMET, TTCs (technical training centres), foreign employers and immigration authorities will be connected on the Overseas Employment Platform (OEP).

headline_en: More than 2.5 billion dollars in remittance for two months running
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data show expatriates sent 256 crore 34 lakh US dollars in October 2025, a little over 7 percent more than October 2024, after 268 crore 58 lakh in September. The article gives the bank-type breakdown, earlier months, the fiscal-year total and the reserve level.

facts.statement: Expatriate Bangladeshis sent 256 crore 34 lakh US dollars in remittance in October 2025, against 239 crore 50 lakh dollars in October 2024, a rise of a little over 7 percent.
Remittance to Bangladesh was 268 crore 58 lakh US dollars in September 2025, 242 crore 18 lakh in August 2025 and 247 crore 80 lakh in July 2025.

Of October 2025 remittance, 47 crore 78 lakh US dollars came through state-owned banks, 183 crore 86 lakh through private banks, 24 crore through Bangladesh Krishi Bank and 66 lakh through foreign banks.
In fiscal year 2024-25 Bangladesh received more than USD 30 billion in remittance, about 6.5 billion or 27 percent more than in 2023-24.
With good remittance inflow, Bangladesh Bank's gross foreign exchange reserves again crossed USD 32 billion (3,200 crore dollars), and import letter-of-credit opening also rose.

headline_en: IOM starts mobile film show on safe migration
summary_en: IOM began a travelling film show called 'Cinema Angina' to raise awareness of safe migration, running 13 October to 17 November 2025 in Madaripur, Faridpur and Shariatpur with support from Italy's foreign ministry. It aims to warn young people about the risks of unsafe migration and promote skills, entrepreneurship and safe migration options.

facts.statement: The International Organization for Migration (IOM) is running a mobile film show called 'Cinema Angina' (সিনেমা আঙিনা) on safe migration from 13 October to 17 November 2025 in 13 municipalities and about 480 villages of Madaripur, Faridpur and Shariatpur districts, with plays, music events, workshops and community discussions, supported by Italy's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation.

Local technical training centres (TTCs), District Employment and Manpower Offices and the Ministry of Home Affairs will help organise the IOM 'Cinema Angina' events; the aim is to make young people and local communities aware of the risks of unsafe migration and encourage skills development, entrepreneurship and safe migration opportunities.

'Cinema Angina' began in 2002 with Italian cooperation as a social and health awareness campaign and from 2018, in partnership with IOM, became an international campaign on the risks of unsafe migration; it has reached about 2 lakh 43 thousand people through more than 670 shows in six African countries.

Lance Bonneau is named as IOM Bangladesh chief of mission and Salvatore Sortino as director of IOM's Mediterranean coordination office; Sortino said 'Cinema Angina' is a new experience in Bangladesh, where the context differs from Africa.

headline_en: 25 held in the UAE to be freed soon, government hopeful
summary_en: The Expatriates' Welfare Ministry said 188 of the Bangladeshi migrants detained in the UAE over protests during the July uprising have returned home, but 25 remain in Abu Dhabi prison. It lists the diplomatic and legal steps taken for their release, including hiring a law firm, which says state-security cases make the process slow.

facts.statement: Of the Bangladeshi migrants detained in the UAE at various times during the July mass uprising, 188 have returned to Bangladesh, while 25 are still held in Abu Dhabi prison; the government said it was hopeful of their release soon.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: In the first round, a UAE court sentenced 57 Bangladeshis detained over protests in the UAE: three to life imprisonment, 53 to 10 years and one to 11 years.

On 28 August 2024 Chief Adviser Professor Muhammad Yunus spoke by phone with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and asked for the Bangladeshis' sentences to be pardoned; the UAE responded, and freed migrants began returning to Bangladesh from the first week of September 2024.

For the remaining prisoners, the Bangladesh embassy in Abu Dhabi took the initiative on 22 April 2025 and sent a list to the UAE foreign ministry seeking help; in May ambassador Tareq Ahmed raised it with senior UAE foreign ministry officials; on 1 July 2025 the embassy sent another note verbale seeking consular access.

On 8 July 2025 a law firm named Hamdan Al Kaabi (হামদান আল কাবি) was engaged to speed up the release of the 25 Bangladeshi prisoners in the UAE; the firm said that because the detainees face state-security related cases the legal steps are time-consuming and must follow various state formalities.

On 7 August 2025 the Bangladesh ambassador met UAE foreign minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan and handed over a hard copy list of the 25 prisoners with contact details; on 21 September adviser Asif Nazrul sent a request letter to UAE Minister of Justice Abdullah bin Sultan bin Awad Al Nuaimi; on 22 September the UAE foreign ministry asked the embassy for the 25 people's passport copies and visa numbers, which were sent by note verbale on 30 September 2025.
More than 10 lakh (1 million) Bangladeshis are in the United Arab Emirates.

headline_en: Suicidal tendency rising among Bangladeshis abroad
summary_en: A reader's letter from a Bangladeshi worker in Doha argues that suicides among migrants are rising and names three main causes: marital breakdown from years of separation, pressure to repay high-interest migration loans, and abusive conditions for women domestic workers in the Middle East. He asks for a migrant help app, skills-based visas, lower migration cost and a second post-mortem in Bangladesh for disputed deaths.

facts.statement: A 2024 statistic cited in the letter says Bangladesh has more than 1 crore 35 lakh expatriates, of whom more than 30 lakh are in Saudi Arabia.
facts.source_in_article: Letter writer Minhaj Bin Mahbub, citing an unnamed 2024 statistic

facts.statement: The letter writer, himself a migrant in Doha, says most men who die by suicide abroad are married; many stay abroad for years, sometimes unable to visit home for years because they have no visa or iqama, which breaks down the marriage.
facts.source_in_article: Minhaj Bin Mahbub, migrant worker in Doha (opinion)

facts.statement: The letter says many migrants come on compound or high-interest loans and cannot repay; creditors pressure the family, the pressure returns to the migrant, and some take their own lives.

The letter says brokers in Bangladesh make attractive promises but women who come to Middle Eastern countries on domestic work visas mostly face problems: no fixed hours or type of work, many are not paid properly, some receive sexual propositions, many suffer physical and mental abuse, and brokers also force some women into prostitution after promising other work.

The letter says families of many migrants who die by suicide abroad believe they were murdered, pointing to wound marks on the body; most such disputed cases are domestic workers, and he says a second post-mortem should be done when the body arrives in Bangladesh.

The letter writer proposes a government migrant-support app through which migrants can report any problem by phone so the Bangladesh embassy can act, training aspirants in one skill and permitting visas for that work, and lowering migration cost.

key_quote_bn: অনেক প্রবাসী চক্রবৃদ্ধি সুদে অথবা উচ্চ সুদে লোন করে এখানে আসেন, তিনি সেই লোনের টাকা শোধ করতে পারেন না, পাওনাদার পরিবারকে নানা রকম চাপ দেয়।

headline_en: 'Bomber' Faisal's reign of terror in Kalkini: people driven out, even police afraid
summary_en: A report on Faisal Talukdar, a gang leader in Kalkini, Madaripur, accused in a triple murder and many other cases. Victim families told Prothom Alo that he began in crime through human trafficking: for 15 years he worked for Libya-based trafficker Miraj Hawladar, trafficking people and collecting ransom from families of local youths held captive in Libya. The rest of the article concerns local violence.

facts.statement: At least 10 affected families told Prothom Alo that Miraj Hawladar, son of Hachen Hawladar of Mridhakandi, Shikarmangal union, Kalkini, Madaripur, lives in Libya and is a leading member of a human-trafficking gang there; for 15 years he used Faisal Talukdar of Kalkini for human trafficking and for collecting ransom from the families of local young men held captive in Libya.
facts.source_in_article: At least 10 affected families, to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: The pattern described in Kalkini, Madaripur: a trafficker based in Libya holds local youths captive there while a local associate in the home area collects ransom money from their families.

Faisal Talukdar (38), son of Bazlu Talukdar of Kalai Sardarerchar, Kalkini, has 15 cases at Kalkini police station since 2006 (robbery, mugging, looting, attacks, explosions, murder, rape, extortion) plus 7 more filed after 5 August (2024); he was arrested in a triple murder case (bomb killing of UP member Ataur Rahman and two others on 27 December 2024, in which he is accused no. 18), spent about seven months in jail and has been out on bail for a month and a half; police say there is no arrest warrant against him. No human-trafficking case is mentioned.
facts.source_in_article: Kalkini police station, district police and upazila administration sources; OC K M Sohel Rana

headline_en: Human smuggling to Japan through a fake football team; broker arrested in Pakistan
summary_en: Pakistan's Federal Investigation Agency arrested Waqas Ali of Pasrur, Sialkot, who posed as a football agent and sent Pakistani migrants to Japan disguised as footballers using forged papers. The people involved are Pakistani, not Bangladeshi; the article is recorded for the method. Seventeen went on 15-day visas in January 2024 and did not return; a second group of 22 was turned back at a Japanese airport in June 2025.

facts.statement: In Pakistan, Waqas Ali posed as a football agent, set up a fake club called 'Golden Football Trial' and sent irregular migrants (Pakistanis) to Japan dressed as football players, using fake Pakistan Football Federation (PFF) registration and letters and a forged no-objection letter of the foreign ministry.
Waqas Ali took 40 to 45 lakh rupees (Pakistani) from each participant in the fake football team scheme to Japan.
Using an invitation letter of 'Boavista Football Club', Waqas Ali obtained 15-day Japan visas for 17 migrants; they went to Japan on 1 January 2024 and did not return to Pakistan.

On 15 June 2025 Waqas Ali tried to send a fake 22-member football team to Japan; all wore football kit and claimed to be PFF players with forged foreign ministry no-objection letters, but Japanese immigration detected the fraud during questioning at the airport and sent them back.
facts.source_in_article: FIA officials, via Gulf News and Dawn

facts.statement: The FIA Gujranwala zone detained Waqas Ali, a resident of Pasrur in Sialkot, on 15 September 2025; zone director Muhammad Bin Ashraf told Dawn a case has been filed and investigation is under way.
facts.source_in_article: Muhammad Bin Ashraf, FIA Gujranwala zone director, via Dawn

summary_en: A short text accompanying a video report: Expatriates' Welfare Adviser Asif Nazrul said at a press conference on the ministry's one-year activities that, as demand for unskilled workers is falling, the government is focusing on sending skilled workers. The headline says the emphasis is on Europe and Japan.

facts.statement: At a press conference on Wednesday 20 August 2025 on the Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry's one year of activities, adviser Professor Asif Nazrul said the government is focusing on sending skilled workers because demand for unskilled workers is falling; the headline quotes him as emphasising sending skilled workers to Europe and Japan.

headline_en: We are now ready to hand power to elected representatives: Chief Adviser
summary_en: Speaking to expatriate Bangladeshis in Kuala Lumpur on 12 August 2025, Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus said the government is working to ensure expatriates can vote in the next election, has acted on passport problems, is launching a 'Nagorik Seba Bangladesh' initiative and is building an app for expatriates. Issues raised by migrants in Malaysia included embassy staffing, Graduate Plus visas for Bangladeshi students and regularisation of irregular workers.

facts.statement: Chief Adviser Professor Muhammad Yunus told expatriate Bangladeshis in Kuala Lumpur on Tuesday 12 August 2025 that the government is working to ensure expatriates' voting rights in the coming election and that the Election Commission, with which this was discussed, is preparing.

Yunus said the government acted very quickly to resolve passport-related complications, is taking up the 'Nagorik Seba Bangladesh' (নাগরিক সেবা বাংলাদেশ) initiative to bring all government services to expatriates, and is developing a special app so expatriate Bangladeshis in all countries can stay connected on one platform.
facts.source_in_article: Muhammad Yunus, via press wing release

facts.statement: Problems of Bangladeshis in Malaysia discussed at the Kuala Lumpur meeting included increasing embassy staff, the Graduate Plus visa for Bangladeshi students, and regularising those who have become irregular; no decision or outcome is reported.
Expatriates' Welfare Adviser Asif Nazrul said cooperation in trade and industry had been discussed with the Malaysian authorities; Foreign Adviser Md. Touhid Hossain was also present at the meeting.
facts.source_in_article: Asif Nazrul, via press wing release

headline_en: Protest with four demands including release of expatriates jailed or detained for 'taking part' in the July movement
summary_en: More than a hundred returnee migrants and relatives blocked the road near Hotel InterContinental in Dhaka on 22 June 2025 demanding release of Bangladeshis still jailed in the UAE and Saudi Arabia over July-movement protests, plus recognition, rehabilitation and state listing of affected returnees. They said 189 were freed from UAE prisons and returned, and that a promised rehabilitation has not happened.

facts.statement: Protesters said 189 Bangladeshi migrants jailed in the UAE for joining July-movement protests were released and returned home with the Chief Adviser's help, but migrants are still imprisoned or detained in the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia. (A later ministry release gives the returned number as 188.)

Under the banner 'Jail-returned victim expatriate remittance fighters affected by the July 24 movement', over a hundred people demonstrated in Dhaka on Sunday 22 June 2025 with four demands: quick release of migrants jailed or detained in the UAE and Saudi Arabia in July-movement cases; recognition of affected returnees as 'July expatriate fighters'; rehabilitation of affected returnees; and their inclusion in a state list.

Police stopped the protesters' march toward the Chief Adviser's residence Jamuna in front of Hotel InterContinental; at about 1:30 pm an eight-member delegation went to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs with police help.

Organiser Sagir Talukdar, a UAE returnee, said affected migrant workers had submitted memoranda several times to the Chief Adviser's Office and ministries, and that the Expatriates' Welfare Adviser had promised rehabilitation but it had not been carried out.

facts.statement: Nurun Nahar of Daganbhuiyan upazila, Feni, said her husband has been in a UAE jail since 29 October 2024 for taking part in the July movement and another of her brothers is also held there.

headline_en: Asif Nazrul speaks of plan to build a hospital for expatriates
summary_en: At the launch of a skills course for SSC examinees at Tangail TTCs on 31 May 2025, Expatriates' Welfare Adviser Asif Nazrul said he dreams of a hospital for expatriates owned by expatriates. He listed market developments: Eastern Europe (Serbia, Romania) opening, Japan's assurance of taking one lakh workers, Malaysia's assurance, regularisation of irregular workers in Saudi Arabia and Jordan, and efforts to open Bahrain and the UAE.

facts.statement: Adviser Asif Nazrul said on 31 May 2025 that markets in Eastern Europe including Serbia and Romania are opening for Bangladeshi workers.
facts.source_in_article: Asif Nazrul, Expatriates' Welfare Adviser, speaking to journalists in Tangail

facts.statement: Asif Nazrul said Dr Yunus received an assurance from Japan that one lakh (100,000) workers will be taken from Bangladesh.
Asif Nazrul said that when he visited Malaysia, they said they would take the largest number of workers from Bangladesh.
Asif Nazrul said Saudi Arabia and Jordan assured him they would arrange to regularise Bangladeshi workers who were irregular, and have already started doing so.
Asif Nazrul said Bangladesh is trying to get Bahrain and the UAE opened (for Bangladeshi workers).

A skills development course for SSC examinees was launched at the Tangail, Nagarpur and Kalihati technical training centres (TTCs): during the three to six idle months after the SSC exam students get training in computer, graphics design and web design; 6,000 students were involved this year, and Asif Nazrul called it a first in Bangladesh.
Asif Nazrul said the international labour market no longer wants semi-skilled or unskilled workers, and without increasing skilled workers the future of the labour market will not be good.
Asif Nazrul said he has a 'dream project' to build a hospital for expatriates that would be owned by expatriates themselves; it is a wish, not an announced project.
Saleh Ahmed Mozaffar is named as director general of the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET) and Md. Rashedul Islam as principal of Tangail TTC.

key_quote_bn: সৌদি, জর্ডানে আমাদের যারা ইরেগুলার ওয়ার্কার ছিল, তাদের রেগুলার করার ব্যবস্থা করবে, এ আশ্বাস আমাকে দিয়েছে এবং অলরেডি করা শুরু করেছে।

headline_en: Formal channels for sending remittance must be made more attractive
summary_en: An analysis of US President Trump's proposal for a 5 percent tax on remittances sent from the US, warning it would cut what families receive and push senders to hundi. It gives figures on US-origin remittance to Bangladesh and urges engaging US policymakers and making formal channels cheaper, faster and easier.

facts.statement: US President Donald Trump recently proposed a 5 percent tax on foreign remittances sent from the United States (a proposal as of May 2025).

In the first nine months of fiscal year 2024-25 migrants sent about USD 3.94 billion (394 crore dollars) from the United States to Bangladesh, more than 18 percent of the country's total remittance; US-origin remittance is now higher than that from many Gulf countries.
In March 2025 Bangladesh received a record USD 3.29 billion (329 crore dollars) in remittance.

The writer says recent remittance growth is due to a comparatively favourable exchange rate and a narrower gap between formal and informal channel rates; a US remittance tax would directly cut what families receive and could increase use of unregulated methods like hundi. Recommended: engage US policymakers, make banking and digital channels easier, faster and cheaper, run awareness campaigns, monitor informal channels and implement the market-based exchange rate.

He ordered the minister for employment and immigration to investigate and urged employers to improve housing and meet basic needs urgently.

facts.statement: 26 Bangladeshi workers employed at a local supermarket in Fiji's Central Division complained directly to Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka that their living conditions are unsuitable, food supply is insufficient and various terms of their employment have been violated.

On the basis of the 26 Bangladeshi workers' complaints, Fiji's Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka directed the minister for employment and immigration to investigate, and urged employers to urgently improve the workers' accommodation and ensure their basic needs.

facts.statement: Rabuka said no worker should live in conditions that compromise their dignity, and that as Fijians also work abroad, foreign nationals working in Fiji should be treated the same way Fiji wants its own citizens treated.

headline_en: Salute, expatriate brothers and sisters...
summary_en: A column praising migrants for lifting remittance toward USD 3 billion in March 2025 and rebuilding reserves after the July 2024 remittance boycott. It asks whether migrants get due respect, citing 19,387 migrants returned dead in 2019 to 2023, poor embassy service, airport mistreatment, middlemen on air tickets and untrained departures, and credits the ministry with lowering ticket prices and improving the airport.

facts.statement: From 2019 to 2023, 19,387 Bangladeshi migrants returned home as dead bodies.
facts.source_in_article: Columnist Subail Bin Alam (no source given)

facts.statement: The columnist says remittance had almost touched the USD 3 billion mark for the month (full data to 31 March pending) after having just reached 2.5 billion in October (2024); the World Bank forecast at budget time was 24 billion for the year.
According to the central bank, Bangladesh's gross reserves rose to USD 25.44 billion on Thursday 27 March (2025); by the IMF's BPM-6 method reserves were USD 20.29 billion.

The columnist says the lowest remittance in recent political history came in July 2024 during the 'remittance boycott' of the July uprising, and the then Awami League government campaigned through embassies.

Protesting migrants were arrested in the UAE and faced long sentences; the columnist says the Awami League government did not stand by them, and they were freed through Professor Muhammad Yunus's efforts after the interim government took office.

The columnist says migrants (over one crore, without voting rights) mostly do not get proper service from embassies; middlemen take much of their money, for example on flight tickets; many leave without minimum training, not knowing how to communicate; bodies of those who die on illegal routes do not come home; and being cheated abroad is frequent.

The columnist says labour migrants are singled out by dress or speech for long lines and extra checking, often face bad behaviour at Dhaka airport, and there are huge lines for Biman tickets in Dubai; he recounts meeting a Bangladeshi returning from the Middle East on an Air India flight who was crying from hunger with no money to buy food.
The columnist says the expatriates' welfare ministry is trying: it has reduced ticket prices, the airport situation is better than before, and plans for some training and policy-making are under way.

The columnist says Pakistan's remittance was below Bangladesh's until 2020 and has now passed 30 billion; he argues Bangladesh must send people for 'white collar' jobs and that 35 billion is not impossible.

key_quote_bn: ২০১৯ থেকে ২০২৩ সাল পর্যন্ত প্রবাসে থেকে লাশ হয়ে ফিরেছেন ১৯ হাজার ৩৮৭ জন।

headline_en: Bangladeshi credit cards spend the most abroad in the United States
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank's latest report shows the US became the top source of remittance to Bangladesh after the August 2024 political change, with 49 crore dollars in February 2025, and is also where Bangladeshi credit cards are used most. India fell from first to sixth in card spending in six months after it tightened visas for Bangladeshis, with Thailand and Malaysia rising as alternatives for treatment and travel.

facts.statement: In February 2025 the United States was the top source of remittance to Bangladesh with 49 crore US dollars; since the political change of August 2024 the US has overtaken Middle Eastern countries as the top remittance source.

After the political change of August 2024 India tightened visa issuance for Bangladeshis, and travel to India for tourism and medical treatment fell significantly; Thailand and Malaysia have become major alternatives for treatment and travel.

Bangladeshi credit card spending abroad was BDT 446 crore in January 2025 (BDT 492 crore in December 2024); the US was highest at BDT 69 crore, Thailand second at BDT 64 crore, Singapore third at BDT 38 crore; the US, Thailand, Singapore, Malaysia and the UK together accounted for BDT 239 crore.
In June 2024 Bangladeshis spent the most by credit card in India (BDT 92 crore, against BDT 77 crore in the US that month); within six months India fell from first to sixth place.

key_quote_bn: এ মাসে দেশটি থেকে সর্বোচ্চ ৪৯ কোটি মার্কিন ডলারের প্রবাসী আয় এসেছে।

headline_en: One person brought in BDT 730 crore in the name of remittance: NBR chairman
summary_en: NBR chairman Md. Abdur Rahman Khan said a businessman brought BDT 730 crore into Bangladesh claiming it as tax-free wage-earner remittance, abusing the tax exemption and cash incentive meant for migrants. He restated that remittance sent through banking channels is tax-free by law and carries a 2.5 percent government incentive.

facts.statement: Remittance sent to Bangladesh through legal (banking) channels is exempt from income tax under law, and the government additionally pays a 2.5 percent incentive (cash assistance) on remittance.
facts.source_in_article: NBR chairman Md. Abdur Rahman Khan; reporter

facts.statement: NBR chairman Md. Abdur Rahman Khan said on Monday 17 March 2025 that a businessman brought BDT 730 crore into the country claiming it was wage-earner remittance and therefore tax-free, taking the tax exemption and cash incentive in breach of the rules; he did not give the name or the time, and said action must be taken and the name would be known after that.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Abdur Rahman Khan, NBR chairman, at an ERF and BCS tax cadre meeting at Rajswa Bhaban, Agargaon

facts.statement: The NBR chairman said there are 1 crore 13 lakh TIN holders but only 40 lakh file returns; in future tax information (deposits, tax deducted at source) will be pulled automatically from banks through an API when filing returns.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Abdur Rahman Khan, NBR chairman

named_actors.name: Unnamed businessman
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Brought in BDT 730 crore as claimed tax-free wage-earner remittance; NBR chairman says rules were breached
named_actors.status: NBR says action will be taken; name withheld

key_quote_bn: বর্তমানে বৈধ চ্যানেলে প্রবাসী আয় দেশে পাঠানোর ক্ষেত্রে করমুক্তি সুবিধা রয়েছে। এ ছাড়া প্রবাসী আয়ে সরকার আড়াই শতাংশ প্রণোদনা বা নগদ সহায়তা দিচ্ছে।
